name: Basecamp
tagline: Opinionated project management with to-dos, message boards, schedules, and chat in one project container.
description: Basecamp keeps to-dos, message boards, schedules, and team chat inside one deliberately simple project container at a recorded price band.
pros: Message boards and campfire chat sit inside the project, so a discussion stays next to the to-do list it concerns
Another pricing record in this repository covers the whole team with a single flat price, so adding people does not multiply the bill
A project ships with a fixed set of tools, so a team can start posting without an administrator modeling a workflow first
Hill Chart-style progress gives a fast read on which lists are still being figured out and which are in execution
Rated 4.1 out of 5 from 1,820 reviews in this repository's recorded data
cons: The pricing record disagrees with itself: this page's band is per user while another file describes a flat monthly price, so budgeting needs vendor confirmation
No dependency scheduling, resource leveling, or portfolio roll-up is part of the published shape, so cross-project planning happens in another tool
Progress depends on people marking Hill Charts and closing to-dos, so status is judgment rather than a computed roll-up across projects

features.name: To-do lists with owners
features.description: Work is tracked as lists of to-dos inside each project, with people assigned and dates attached, which is the layer the published model is built around.

features.name: Message boards
features.description: Discussion threads are kept with the project. The remote-team guide in this repository records message boards as one of the two communication surfaces placed in project context.

features.name: Campfire group chat
features.description: Campfire provides real-time chat inside the same project, recorded alongside message boards in the remote-team buying guide held in this repository.

features.name: Project schedule
features.description: Each project carries a schedule of dated events and deadlines, so timing lives beside the to-dos and threads it governs.

features.name: Hill Chart progress view
features.description: Work is shown moving from an uncertain uphill phase into a downhill execution phase, with the team marking position rather than a formula computing it.

features.name: Documents and file storage
features.description: Files and documents are stored inside the project they belong to, keeping reference material beside the lists and threads that use it.

features.name: Automatic check-ins
features.description: Recurring written check-ins ask a team the same questions on a schedule, collecting answers in one place instead of holding a status meeting.

features.name: Client access to projects
features.description: Clients can be given a view of a project, so agency-style feedback and files live in the same container as the team's own discussion.

content.title: How Basecamp organizes a project
content.body: A Basecamp project is the container for one piece of work: to-do lists with owners and dates, a message board for discussion, a schedule, and a place for documents and files. Rather than asking an administrator to model custom fields, statuses, and dependencies first, the product ships a fixed set of tools per project and expects a team to start filling them in. This repository records Basecamp as a simple project management and team communication platform, and the project container is where those two jobs meet. Everything else in the product is a variation on that container.

content.title: Message boards, campfire, and the async default
content.body: Communication is stored in the project rather than in a separate chat product. The remote-team buying guide in this repository records Basecamp as particularly well designed for asynchronous communication because it puts message boards and its campfire chat directly into project context, so a discussion sits beside the to-do list it concerns. Threads stay readable after the fact instead of scrolling away, which is the practical difference between a project record and a chat channel. For distributed groups it also removes the recurring argument about which channel a decision was made in.

content.title: The Hill Chart and how progress gets read
content.body: Basecamp reports progress informally rather than computing it. The product's published Hill Chart approach shows work moving out of an uncertain phase, where the shape of the problem is still being worked out, into a downhill phase where execution is understood, and each to-do list's position is marked by judgment. Status therefore comes from what people say about their work. The list below is the fixed tool set that carries a project from intake to that weekly read.
items: To-do lists with assignees and due dates
A message board kept with the project
A schedule of dated events and deadlines
Documents and files stored beside the work
Hill Chart-style progress marked by the team

content.title: What Basecamp deliberately leaves out
content.body: Basecamp's design assumes most teams do not carry the machinery that heavier project tools carry. Its published feature set centers on to-dos, message boards, schedules, and check-ins rather than on dependency scheduling, resource leveling, or portfolio roll-ups, so progress is read off completion marks instead of calculated. Teams that manage cross-project critical paths or capacity planning will keep those views in another system. That is a scope choice rather than a gap the product is racing to close, and it is why Basecamp keeps appearing here as the simple option in a field of configurable ones.

content.title: The price record, and where it disagrees
content.body: This page records Basecamp as paid with a list price band of $15/user/mo, and that is the only figure quoted here. A separate file in this repository describes a different shape: a flat monthly price covering unlimited users rather than a rate multiplied by headcount. The two records cannot both be current, so treat the band as indicative and confirm the live model with the vendor before budgeting. Flat pricing is the philosophy the product is known for, which makes the discrepancy worth resolving early rather than at renewal.

content.title: Deployment, storage, and the certifications not on file
content.body: Basecamp is delivered as a hosted service, so project data sits on the vendor's infrastructure and reaches people through browsers and mobile clients. The dataset behind this page stores no compliance certification for Basecamp and this review states none; readers check the vendor’s published documentation for the current position. For teams putting client work and internal discussion in the same place, the questions worth pressing are about data residency, how long deleted threads are retained, and what export produces when a project is wound down.

content.title: How this repository pairs Basecamp
content.body: Thirteen comparison files in this repository place Basecamp opposite other products. Ten are same-shape tools, Airtable, Asana, ClickUp, Confluence, Jira, Linear, Monday.com, Smartsheet, Trello, and Wrike, where the argument is about how much structure a project needs. The other three pair it with Calendly, Google Meet, and Greenhouse, which sell scheduling, meetings, and recruiting rather than project tracking. The split is informative: Basecamp tends to be measured against configurable tools as the fixed alternative, and against the rest as a category anchor.

content.title: Smartsheet, Wrike, and the wider field
content.body: Smartsheet, which this repository pairs with Basecamp on its own comparison page, is spreadsheet-shaped: rows, formulas, Gantt views, and governance aimed at enterprise standardization. Wrike, also compared here, is the configurable middle, with request forms and reporting depth for teams that will model their process first. Basecamp is the opposite pole, a fixed project container with a communication layer, bought when a team wants fewer decisions. The Basecamp alternatives file names ClickUp, Trello, Airtable, and Wrike as the closest substitutes on record.

content.title: Who should run projects in Basecamp
content.body: Basecamp fits small and mid-sized teams whose work is coordination rather than computation: agencies, startups, and departments that want a shared place for discussion, files, and to-dos without an administrator maintaining a workflow. It fits groups that communicate asynchronously and want the conversation stored with the work. It does not fit program managers who need dependencies, capacity, or cross-project reporting inside the same tool. The assessment above rests on documented product information and the records this repository holds for Basecamp, not on any use of the product. Those records show 4.1 out of 5 from 1,820 reviews.

faqs.question: Does Basecamp charge per person?
faqs.answer: This page records a band of $15/user/mo, while another file in this repository describes a flat monthly price covering unlimited users. The two records disagree on shape, so confirm the current model with the vendor.

faqs.question: Can Basecamp show dependencies or a Gantt timeline?
faqs.answer: Not in anything published about the product or recorded here. Basecamp reports progress through to-do completion and Hill Chart-style marks rather than through dependency scheduling.

faqs.question: Where does team conversation happen in Basecamp?
faqs.answer: Inside the project. This repository records message boards and campfire chat sitting directly in project context, which is why its remote-team guide recommends the product for asynchronous work.

faqs.question: Is Basecamp a good fit for client or agency work?
faqs.answer: The shape suits it: projects hold files, boards, and schedules in one container. This repository files Basecamp in its startup, agile, and remote-team lists, where client-facing work is common.

faqs.question: How is Basecamp different from Smartsheet and Wrike?
faqs.answer: Smartsheet is spreadsheet-shaped and Wrike is configurable, with request forms and reporting depth. Basecamp is fixed and opinionated, with communication built into the project instead of configuration.

author: Sarah Chen
learningCurve: Low, because the fixed tool set per project means a team can create a project and start posting without an administrator modeling workflows first
whoShouldUse: Small and mid-sized teams that want one container for discussion, files, to-dos, and schedules, and that would rather accept a fixed structure than configure a workflow: agencies, startups, and distributed groups coordinating rather than computing.
whoShouldNotUse: Program managers who need dependency scheduling, resource leveling, or portfolio reporting in the same tool; buyers who cannot confirm the current pricing model with the vendor; and organizations that require documented compliance certifications before rollout.
